summary: Tractate Yoma daf 87a covers: Going willingly to die vs. against will: a halachic distinction; YK does not atone without appeasement of the one wronged; need to ask forgiveness directly; Yom Kippur atones for sins against God; does NOT atone for sins against another person; YK atones for communal sins between people toward God; One who angers a friend - even verbally - must appease them directly.

display.whats: Rava's self-caution before sitting in judgment, and his and Rav Zutra's warnings against the danger of public honor
display.hint: What does Rava say about his own mortality before sitting in judgment, and what lesson does he draw when a crowd follows him in honor?
display.title: Rava's Self-Admonition Before Judging

learning.ahaMoment: Rava treats the anxiety of judging as itself protective: naming the risk of ruling wrongly keeps him humble, and when honor follows him instead, he reaches for the same kind of caution.
learning.memoryAnchor: Rava before judging: 'of his own will he goes to die... if only his entrance were like his exit.' Seeing a crowd follow him in honor: 'though his excellency mounts to the heavens, he shall perish forever like his dung' (Job 20:6-7).
learning.learnerQuestion: Does it matter halakhically whether a person goes to their death willingly or is forced against their will?
learning.coreTension: Between the fear appropriate to sitting in judgment, where an erring judge is answerable to Heaven, and the danger of the honor a judge or teacher receives, which can lead just as easily to downfall.
learning.coreMove: Rava recites a self-admonition before judging, framing the act as a kind of death he risks for the sake of ruling correctly, hoping to leave the court no worse than he entered it. When a crowd instead follows him in honor, he applies a different verse warning that unchecked honor leads to ruin, and Rav Zutra, carried on shoulders while teaching, recites a matching verse about the impermanence of power to guard against the same danger.

takeaway.text: A judge or teacher must guard against two opposite dangers, the anxiety of getting a ruling wrong and the arrogance public honor can produce, and each danger calls for its own verse of self-caution.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may read Rava's 'of his own will he goes to die' as literal danger to his life; it is a rhetorical self-admonition about the gravity of judging, paired with a separate caution about honor, not a statement about physical risk.

argumentFlow.label: Rava's words before judging; the danger of honor
argumentFlow.speaker: Rava / Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rava, going to judge, said of himself: of his own will he goes to die, he does not do his household's will, and he returns empty-handed - if only his entrance were like his exit. Seeing a crowd following him in his honor, he applied 'though his excellency mounts to the heavens... he shall perish forever like his dung' (Job 20:6-7): honor can lead to a person's downfall. And when Rav Zutra was carried on shoulders while teaching, he recited 'for power is not forever, nor does the crown endure for all generations' (Proverbs 27:24) to guard against arrogance.

misconceptions.misconception: The Sages embraced the public honor that came with their authority.
misconceptions.correction: They actively warned themselves against it, reciting verses on the impermanence of power and the downfall that honor can bring, to stay humble in positions of authority.

visualizableElements.item: Rava's self-admonition before judging and his warning against the danger of honor

quizSeeds.question: Why did Rava and Rav Zutra recite verses warning against honor when they were elevated?
quizSeeds.answer: To guard against arrogance. Rava, seeing crowds follow him, cited Job 20:6-7 that honor can bring one's downfall; Rav Zutra, carried on shoulders, cited Proverbs 27:24 that power and crown do not endure forever.

quizSeeds.question: What attitude toward judging does Rav's and Rava's self-statement express?
quizSeeds.answer: That judging is grave and perilous: a judge who errs is liable to Heaven, earns no pay, and neglects his household. They approached the role with humility and fear rather than a sense of honor.

sugyot.finalRuling: Before judging, Rava reminds himself of the gravity and personal risk of the task; when honored by a crowd instead, he and Rav Zutra each apply a verse cautioning that unchecked honor, like power, does not last and can lead to downfall.

display.whats: This-worldly honor for the wicked and this-worldly punishment for the righteous, and how merit and guilt extend to descendants and to communal leaders
display.hint: Why does the Gemara treat being honored in this world as bad news for a wicked person like Ahab, and being punished here as good news for a righteous person like Moses?
display.title: Honor and Punishment in This World

learning.ahaMoment: Reward and punishment aren't simply about fairness in this life, they function as an accounting mechanism: this-worldly consequences settle a person's account early, for better or worse, changing what remains for the World to Come.
learning.memoryAnchor: Ahab honored here lost his World to Come; Moses punished here kept his. Aaron's sons kept the priesthood on his merit; Canaan's children stayed slaves for his guilt.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why does Yom Kippur not atone for interpersonal sins unless the wronged person is directly appeased?
learning.coreTension: Between the instinct that being honored is good and being punished is bad, and the Gemara's reversal: for the wicked, this-worldly honor comes at the cost of the World to Come, while for the righteous, this-worldly punishment protects it.
learning.coreMove: Expounding 'it is not good to favor the wicked,' the Gemara reads the verse as saying it is bad for the wicked to be honored unpunished here, illustrated by Ahab, whose humbling deferred but did not cancel his punishment, and good for the righteous to be punished here, illustrated by Moses, whose barring from the land settled his account early. It then extends the principle across generations, the righteous earning merit for their descendants (Aaron's sons spared through his merit) and the wicked condemning theirs (Canaan's children left as slaves), and finally to communal leaders: one who brings merit to the public is protected from sin so as not to be punished while his students are rewarded, and the reverse for one who leads the public astray.

takeaway.text: This-worldly reward and punishment function as a kind of accounting that can protect or endanger a person's ultimate portion, and this same logic of earned protection or earned liability extends across generations and to those who influence the public.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may assume being honored is simply good and being punished is simply bad; the Gemara shows both can carry the opposite ultimate significance depending on whether the person is righteous or wicked.

argumentFlow.label: Better for the wicked not to be honored
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: 'It is not good to favor the wicked' (Proverbs 18:5) - it is not good for the wicked to be honored and unpunished in this world. It was bad for Ahab to be honored here: because he humbled himself, 'I will not bring the evil in his days' (I Kings 21:29) - and he thereby lost his share in the World to Come, his account settled in this world.

argumentFlow.label: Good for the righteous not to be honored
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The verse's continuation: 'to turn aside the righteous in judgment' - it is good for the righteous NOT to be honored and to be punished in this world for their sins. It was good for Moses not to be honored: 'because you did not believe in Me' (Numbers 20:12) - had he believed, his time to leave the world would not yet have come. Punishment here preserves the World to Come.

argumentFlow.label: The righteous earn merit for generations
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Fortunate are the righteous: they earn merit not only for themselves but for their children and descendants forever. Several sons of Aaron deserved to be burned like Nadav and Avihu ('the sons of Aaron who were left,' implying others nearly were not), but their father's merit protected them and their line stayed priests.

argumentFlow.label: The wicked condemn their descendants
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Conversely, woe to the wicked: they render liable not only themselves but their descendants forever. Canaan had children fit to be great Torah teachers - like Tavi, Rabban Gamliel's wise servant - but their father's guilt left them slaves.

argumentFlow.label: One who benefits or harms the public
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Whoever brings merit to the public is shielded from sin, so he will not be in Gehenna while his students are in Eden ('You will not abandon my soul to the grave'). Whoever leads the public to sin is barely given the chance to repent, so he will not be in Eden while his students are in Gehenna ('a man laden with the blood of any person shall flee to the pit; none will support him').

misconceptions.misconception: Worldly honor and ease for the wicked signal God's favor.
misconceptions.correction: The sugya teaches the opposite: honor and unpunished ease for the wicked, like Ahab's, settle their reward in this world and cost them the World to Come. Suffering for the righteous is actually 'good.'

visualizableElements.item: The this-worldly honor/punishment reversal for the wicked and righteous, extended to descendants and communal leaders

quizSeeds.question: Why is it considered 'good' for the righteous to suffer and not be honored in this world?
quizSeeds.answer: Because punishment in this world settles their account here and preserves their share in the World to Come. Moses' not being honored, and his punishment, are examples - had he not been held accountable, his time to leave the world would not yet have come.

quizSeeds.question: What is the fate of one who causes the public to sin versus one who brings merit to the public?
quizSeeds.answer: One who brings the public merit is protected from sin, so he won't be in Gehenna while his students are in Eden. One who causes the public to sin is barely allowed to repent, so he won't be in Eden while his students are in Gehenna.

sugyot.finalRuling: This-worldly honor is bad for the wicked, since it forfeits their World to Come, while this-worldly punishment is good for the righteous, since it preserves theirs; this same principle of earned protection or earned liability extends to a person's descendants and to those who influence the public for merit or for sin.

display.whats: The Mishnah's doubled 'I will sin and repent' phrase, and why relying on Yom Kippur in advance forfeits its atonement even according to Rabbi's lenient view
display.hint: Why does the Mishnah state 'I will sin and repent' twice, and how does the Gemara reconcile its ruling that reliance on Yom Kippur cancels atonement with Rabbi's own view that Yom Kippur atones even without repentance?
display.title: Exploiting Repentance or Yom Kippur Forfeits Atonement

learning.ahaMoment: Planning to exploit forgiveness is what disqualifies it, not the sin itself: the same repentance or the same Yom Kippur that would otherwise atone loses its power specifically when it is being used in advance as a license.
learning.memoryAnchor: Rav Huna in Rav's name: repeating a sin makes it feel 'as if permitted.' Even Rabbi, who holds YK atones without repentance, agrees that counting on YK in advance cancels its atonement.
learning.learnerQuestion: What is the scope of Yom Kippur's direct atonement power?
learning.coreTension: Between the Mishnah's ruling that presuming on future repentance or Yom Kippur forfeits atonement, and Rabbi's own more lenient position elsewhere that Yom Kippur atones even without repentance at all.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara first explains the doubled phrase 'I will sin and repent': it is repeated because repeating a sin itself changes its character, making it feel permitted, which is why deliberate repetition specifically closes off repentance. It then reconciles the Mishnah's ruling that relying on Yom Kippur to atone leaves a person unatoned with Rabbi's own broader position: even Rabbi agrees that when a sin is committed precisely because the person is counting on Yom Kippur in advance, that specific reliance forfeits the atonement Yom Kippur would otherwise provide.

takeaway.text: Atonement, whether through repentance or Yom Kippur, is forfeited specifically when it is planned on in advance as a license to sin, even under views that would otherwise grant it very broadly.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may think the Mishnah simply contradicts Rabbi's lenient view that Yom Kippur atones without repentance; the Gemara shows both can be true because the disqualifying factor is the advance reliance on atonement, not repentance's absence.

argumentFlow.label: Why 'I will sin and repent' is doubled
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav (via Rav Huna)
argumentFlow.text: The Mishnah says one who plans 'I will sin and repent, I will sin and repent' is denied the chance to repent. Why state it twice? Per Rav Huna in Rav's name: once a person commits a sin and repeats it, it becomes 'as if permitted' to him. The doubled phrase mirrors how repeating the sin makes it harder to abandon.

argumentFlow.label: 'I will sin and Yom Kippur will atone' - even per Rabbi
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Mishnah says one who relies on Yom Kippur to atone is not atoned. This seems to clash with Rabbi, who held Yom Kippur atones even without repentance. The Gemara answers: even Rabbi agrees that when one sins precisely because he is counting on Yom Kippur, that atonement is forfeited. Exploiting atonement as a license cancels it.

misconceptions.misconception: Since Rabbi holds Yom Kippur atones even without repentance, it must atone even for one who sins counting on it.
misconceptions.correction: Even Rabbi agrees that sinning specifically in reliance on Yom Kippur forfeits its atonement. The license-to-sin attitude is the exception to his rule.

visualizableElements.item: The Mishnah's doubled sin-and-repent phrase and the advance-reliance exception to atonement

quizSeeds.question: Why does the Mishnah repeat 'I will sin and I will repent' twice?
quizSeeds.answer: Per Rav Huna in Rav's name: once a sin is repeated it becomes 'as if permitted' to the person, so it is far harder to abandon. The doubled phrase reflects how repetition entrenches the sin.

quizSeeds.question: Does even Rabbi (who holds Yom Kippur atones without repentance) agree that 'I will sin and Yom Kippur will atone' is not atoned?
quizSeeds.answer: Yes. Even Rabbi concedes that when someone sins specifically in reliance on Yom Kippur, the atonement is forfeited. Treating atonement as a license to sin cancels it.

sugyot.finalRuling: Repentance and Yom Kippur's atonement are both forfeited specifically when a person plans in advance to rely on them as a license to sin; even Rabbi, who otherwise holds Yom Kippur atones without repentance, agrees that this advance reliance cancels the atonement.

display.whats: Rav Yosef bar Chavu's challenge that a verse implies prayer alone forgives a sin against a person, and Rabbi Abbahu's two-stage resolution
display.hint: How does Rabbi Abbahu answer Rav Yosef bar Chavu's challenge that a verse about prayer contradicts the rule that sins against a person are not atoned without appeasing that person?
display.title: Prayer and Appeasement for a Sin Against a Person

learning.ahaMoment: The same Hebrew root can mean 'judge' in one half of a verse and 'forgive through prayer' in the other, and choosing between those meanings is what lets Rabbi Abbahu preserve both the Mishnah's rule and the verse's authority.
learning.memoryAnchor: Rav Yosef bar Chavu: doesn't 'ufilelo' mean prayer secures forgiveness even for sins against a person? Rabbi Abbahu's first answer: it means a judge. His second answer, after being pressed: it does mean forgiveness, but only once the victim has been appeased.
learning.learnerQuestion: Are there interpersonal or communal sins that Yom Kippur can atone for without requiring direct human appeasement?
learning.coreTension: Between the Mishnah's rule that a sin against a person cannot be atoned without appeasing that person, and a verse that appears to say prayer alone secures forgiveness even for such a sin.
learning.coreMove: Rav Yosef bar Chavu challenges Rabbi Abbahu with a verse using the root p-l-l for sins against a person, read as 'prayer wins him forgiveness.' Rabbi Abbahu's first answer reads the same root as 'judge,' meaning the verse simply requires a court to adjudicate the claim. Rav Yosef presses further, since that reading would make the verse's second clause, about a sin against God, mean no one can ever judge such a sin, which is absurd. Rabbi Abbahu therefore rereads the whole verse: for a sin against a person, the root does mean forgiveness, but only once the victim has been appeased; for a sin against God, the same root in the second clause means specifically repentance and good deeds, not prayer.

takeaway.text: A single verse can carry two different meanings for its two clauses, and Rabbi Abbahu uses that distinction to preserve both the verse and the rule that sins against a person require appeasing the victim before any prayer or ritual can complete their atonement.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may take the verse at face value as proving prayer alone forgives interpersonal sins; the Gemara's resolution shows the verse's two halves use the same root for different meanings, so it does not override the appeasement requirement.

argumentFlow.label: Does prayer secure forgiveness for wronging a person?
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Yosef bar Chavu
argumentFlow.text: Rav Yosef bar Chavu challenged Rabbi Abbahu from 'if one sins against another, Elohim shall judge him [ufilelo]' (I Samuel 2:25) - reading ufilelo as prayer, implying prayer wins forgiveness even for sins against a person, contradicting the Mishnah. Rabbi Abbahu answered: Elohim here means a judge, and ufilelo means judgment - forgiveness comes only after the court adjudicates the wronged party's claim.

argumentFlow.label: Rereading the verse's second clause
argumentFlow.speaker: Rabbi Abbahu
argumentFlow.text: Rav Yosef pressed: then the clause 'if a man sins against the Lord, who shall entreat [yitpallel] for him?' would mean no one can judge a sin against God. Rabbi Abbahu reread the whole verse: if one sins against another, God forgives him (ufilelo) once he appeases the victim; but if against God, who shall entreat for him? - repentance and good deeds. Here pll means forgiveness, not judgment.

misconceptions.misconception: Prayer to God alone can secure forgiveness for hurting another person.
misconceptions.correction: As Rabbi Abbahu reads the verse, sins against another person require appeasing the victim (or a court ruling) first; only then does God forgive. Prayer alone does not bypass the wronged party.

visualizableElements.item: Rav Yosef bar Chavu's challenge and Rabbi Abbahu's two-stage rereading of the verse's two clauses

quizSeeds.question: How does Rabbi Abbahu first interpret 'Elohim... ufilelo' in I Samuel 2:25 to defend the Mishnah?
quizSeeds.answer: He reads Elohim as 'a judge' and ufilelo as 'judgment.' Forgiveness for wronging another person comes only after justice is done through a court ruling, not through prayer alone, consistent with the Mishnah.

quizSeeds.question: In Rabbi Abbahu's final reading, what does one need to be forgiven for a sin against another person versus against God?
quizSeeds.answer: For a sin against another person, one must appease the victim, after which God forgives. For a sin against God, repentance and good deeds suffice. In this reading the root pll means forgiveness.

sugyot.finalRuling: A sin against a person is not forgiven through prayer alone; Rabbi Abbahu reads the verse's clause about a sin against a person as requiring the victim's appeasement, while its second clause, about a sin against God, refers to repentance and good deeds rather than prayer.

display.whats: One who angers a friend - even verbally - must appease them directly
display.hint: Even verbal harm to another person requires direct appeasement - if someone was insulted or hurt by words alone, the speaker must go and ask forgiveness.
display.title: Verbal Harm Also Requires Appeasement

learning.ahaMoment: The Torah takes words seriously enough to require the same repair process as physical harm. The hurt from an insult is real; the repair must be equally real.
learning.memoryAnchor: Verbal insult = physical harm for appeasement purposes: words wound too, and the wronged person must be appeased directly.
learning.learnerQuestion: If someone only insulted or hurt another person verbally (not with a physical act), must they still seek direct appeasement?
learning.coreTension: Between treating verbal harm as somehow less serious (no physical damage occurred) and the principle that words can wound as deeply as actions.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara rules explicitly: even verbal harm to another person requires direct appeasement. Words that insult or hurt another person create a real interpersonal rupture that no internal repentance or YK ritual can repair without the wronged person's direct involvement.

takeaway.text: Verbal harm to another person requires direct appeasement, just as physical harm does; the YK limitation on interpersonal sins applies to word-wounds as much as to physical injuries.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may think verbal harm is less serious and therefore exempt from the appeasement requirement; the Gemara applies the same standard to words as to physical acts.

argumentFlow.label: Even a verbal slight needs appeasement
argumentFlow.speaker: R. Yitzchak
argumentFlow.text: Rabbi Yitzchak: one who wrongs his fellow even only with words must appease him, from 'go, humble yourself and urge your neighbor' (Proverbs 6:1-3). If you owe him money, open your hand and pay; if you wronged him with words, send many friends to ask his forgiveness.

argumentFlow.label: Three rows of three
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Chisda
argumentFlow.text: Rav Chisda: one must appease the offended party with three rows of three people, deriving 'shura' (row) from 'yashor before men' (Job 33:27), where the verse mentions sin three times - so one makes three rows before the person he is asking to forgive.

argumentFlow.label: No more than three times; at the grave if he died
argumentFlow.speaker: R. Yosei bar Chanina
argumentFlow.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina: one should not ask forgiveness more than three times, from the threefold 'please' in 'please forgive... and now please forgive' (Genesis 50:17). After three the offended must relent. And if the wronged party died first, one brings ten people to his grave and says: I sinned against the Lord God of Israel and against this person whom I hurt.

argumentFlow.label: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Abba
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rabbi Yirmeya, having wronged Rabbi Abba, sat at his threshold to beg forgiveness. The maid's dirty water splashed his head; he said 'they made me a trash heap' and applied 'He raises the needy from the trash heap' (Psalms 113:7). Rabbi Abba came out, saying: now I must go appease YOU, citing 'go, humble yourself and urge your neighbor.'

argumentFlow.label: Rabbi Zeira makes himself easy to appease
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: When Rabbi Zeira had a grievance against someone who insulted him, he would pace back and forth in front of the person, presenting himself so it would be easy for the other to come and apologize - lowering the barrier to reconciliation.

argumentFlow.label: Rav and the butcher
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Rav had a grievance against a butcher who would not come apologize. On Yom Kippur eve Rav went to appease HIM. Rav Huna warned: 'Abba is going to kill a man' - the butcher's end will be bad. Rav stood before him; the butcher, splitting an animal's head, looked up and said 'You are Abba? Go, I have nothing to say to you' - and a flying bone struck his throat and killed him, fulfilling Rav Huna's words.

argumentFlow.label: Rav reading before Rabbi
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara turns to another episode: Rav was reciting the Torah portion before Rabbi (continued on 87b), setting up the long account of Rav repeatedly restarting the reading out of respect for arriving scholars.

misconceptions.misconception: It is the offender's job alone to seek reconciliation; the wronged party just waits.
misconceptions.correction: The wronged Sages actively made themselves available - Rabbi Zeira paced before the offender, Rav went to the butcher himself - lowering the barrier so the other could apologize. Reconciliation is a shared effort.

quizSeeds.question: How many times must one ask a person for forgiveness, and what is the source?
quizSeeds.answer: No more than three times, from the threefold 'please' in Joseph's brothers' plea, 'please forgive... and now please forgive' (Genesis 50:17). After three sincere requests, the offended party should relent.

quizSeeds.question: What does one do if the person he wronged has already died?
quizSeeds.answer: He brings ten people to the grave and declares before them: I have sinned against the Lord, God of Israel, and against this person whom I wronged. The public confession at the grave substitutes for appeasing the deceased directly.

quizSeeds.question: What lesson does the story of Rav going to appease the butcher convey?
quizSeeds.answer: That the wronged party - here Rav - took the initiative to seek reconciliation even when it was the offender's duty. It also shows the grave danger of refusing to be appeased: the butcher's contemptuous refusal preceded his sudden death.

sugyot.finalRuling: Even verbal harm to another person requires direct appeasement - if someone was insulted or hurt by words alone, the speaker must go and ask forgivene

rashiTranslations.he: אגב שאני. מאחר שעליו הוא סומך
rashiTranslations.en: 'the case is different on account of relying on it' - since he relies on it

rashiTranslations.he: לחטוא אינו מכפר: והכתיב ופללו
rashiTranslations.en: to sin, it does not atone. 'but is it not written, ufilelo'

rashiTranslations.he: אלהים. וקא סלקא דעתך ופללו לשון
rashiTranslations.en: Elohim' - and you might think that ufilelo is a term of

rashiTranslations.he: תפלה ופיוס הוא שהקב"ה מפללו
rashiTranslations.en: prayer and appeasement, that the Holy One prays for him

rashiTranslations.he: ומפייסו ומכפר לו: מאן אלהים דיין.
rashiTranslations.en: and appeases him and atones for him. 'who is Elohim, a judge' -

rashiTranslations.he: והאי ופללו לשון ונתן בפלילים (שמות
rashiTranslations.en: and this ufilelo is a term like venatan biflilim (Shemot

rashiTranslations.he: כא) הדיין ישפוט ביניהם: אי הכי.
rashiTranslations.en: 21) - the judge shall rule between them. 'if so' -

rashiTranslations.he: דפללו דקרא לשון משפט נינהו אימא
rashiTranslations.en: that ufilelo of the verse is a term of judgment, then say

rashiTranslations.he: סיפא מי יתפלל לו מי ישפטנו בשביל
rashiTranslations.en: the latter clause, who shall pray for him, meaning who shall judge him on behalf of

rashiTranslations.he: המקום וכי אין שלוחין הרבה למקום
rashiTranslations.en: God? But does God not have many agents

rashiTranslations.he: ליפרע הימנו: הכי קאמר. הכי נמי
rashiTranslations.en: to punish him? 'this is what it means' - likewise

rashiTranslations.he: דפילול דקרא לשון פיוס הוא והכי קאמר אם יחטא איש לאיש ופללו
rashiTranslations.en: the pilul of the verse is a term of appeasement, and this is what it says: if a man sins against another man and he appeases him,

rashiTranslations.he: לחבירו וריצהו האלהים ימחול לו: ואם לה' יחטא איש מי יתפלל
rashiTranslations.en: toward his fellow, and satisfies him, God will forgive him. 'but if a man sins against the Lord, who shall pray'

rashiTranslations.he: בעדו. אם אינו שב מעבירות שבידו כך היה עלי הכהן מוכיח
rashiTranslations.en: on his behalf - if he does not repent from the transgressions in his hand. So Eli the Priest used to reprove

rashiTranslations.he: את בניו שישובו מרעתם: בני אם ערבת לרעך תקעת לזר כפיך.
rashiTranslations.en: his sons, that they should repent from their evil. 'my son, if you have guaranteed for your neighbor, you have struck hands for a stranger' -

rashiTranslations.he: בשביל זר לערבו בממון או אם
rashiTranslations.en: on behalf of a stranger, to guarantee him monetarily; or if

rashiTranslations.he: נוקשת באמרי פיך שהקנטתו בדברים
rashiTranslations.en: you were ensnared by the words of your mouth, that you provoked him with words,

rashiTranslations.he: עשה זאת והנצל כי באת בכף רעך על
rashiTranslations.en: do this and save yourself, for you have come into your fellow's grip - regarding

rashiTranslations.he: עסקי ממון: לך התרפס. יד ופרע לו
rashiTranslations.en: monetary matters. 'go, humble yourself' - give a hand and pay him,

rashiTranslations.he: ועל מוקש אמרי פיך אם הקנטתו
rashiTranslations.en: and regarding the snare of the words of your mouth, if you provoked him,

rashiTranslations.he: רהב רעיך הרבה רעים לבקש הימנו
rashiTranslations.en: urhav re'echa - increase friends to seek from him

rashiTranslations.he: מחילה. רעיך בתרא דקרא מלא כתיב
rashiTranslations.en: forgiveness. 're'echa' the second time in the verse is written in full spelling,

rashiTranslations.he: לפי שהוא לשון רבים: בשלש שורות.
rashiTranslations.en: since it is plural. 'in three rows' -

rashiTranslations.he: שלש פעמים יפייסוהו בשלשה אנשים
rashiTranslations.en: three times he should be appeased in the presence of three people,

rashiTranslations.he: בכל פעם שנאמר ישור לשון שורה
rashiTranslations.en: each time, since it says yashor, a term of row,

rashiTranslations.he: ואין שורה פחותה משלשה בני אדם :
rashiTranslations.en: and a row is no fewer than three people.

rashiTranslations.he: חטאתי. הרי פעם אחת וישר העויתי
rashiTranslations.en: 'I have sinned' - this is one time. 'and yashar he'eviti' -

rashiTranslations.he: הרי שתים ולא שוה לי הרי שלשה:
rashiTranslations.en: this is two; 'and it was not equal to me' - this is three.

rashiTranslations.he: אנא שא נא ועתה שא נא. אין נא
rashiTranslations.en: 'please lift up now, and now lift up' - na is nothing

rashiTranslations.he: אלא לשון בקשה: הוה ליה מילתא
rashiTranslations.en: but a term of request. 'there was a matter'

rashiTranslations.he: לר' אבא בהדיה. ר' אבא היה לו
rashiTranslations.en: with Rabbi Abba - Rabbi Abba had

rashiTranslations.he: להתרעם על ר' ירמיה שחטא לו אזל
rashiTranslations.en: cause to complain against Rabbi Yirmiyah, who had sinned against him. Rabbi Yirmiyah went,

rashiTranslations.he: ר' ירמיה איתיב אדשא דר' אבא:
rashiTranslations.en: Rabbi Yirmiyah, and sat at the door of Rabbi Abba's house.

rashiTranslations.he: זרזיפי דמיא. התזת טיפי שופכין
rashiTranslations.en: 'zarzifei demaya' - the spattering of droplets

rashiTranslations.he: שהיתה השפחה שופכת וזרזיפי טיפין
rashiTranslations.en: of wastewater that the maidservant was pouring out, and drops of droplets,

rashiTranslations.he: ודומה לו כרביבים זרזיף ארץ בספר
rashiTranslations.en: similar to it: like showers, zarzif eretz, in the book of

rashiTranslations.he: תהלים (עב) : ממציא נפשיה. לפני
rashiTranslations.en: Tehillim (72). 'presents himself' - before

rashiTranslations.he: מי שחטא לו אולי יבקש ממנו מחילה
rashiTranslations.en: the one who sinned against him, so that perhaps he would seek forgiveness from him

rashiTranslations.he: וימחול לו: חליף ותני. עובר ושונה
rashiTranslations.en: and he would forgive him. 'passes and repeats' - passes over and repeats,

rashiTranslations.he: ומשלש פעמים רבות: בהדי טבחא.
rashiTranslations.en: and does so three or many times. 'with the butcher' -

rashiTranslations.he: הטבח חטא לו: קאזיל אבא.
rashiTranslations.en: the butcher had sinned against him. 'Abba is going' -

rashiTranslations.he: רביה: למקטל נפשיה. עכשיו הוא
rashiTranslations.en: his teacher. 'to kill himself' - now

rashiTranslations.he: מענישו למות: תבר רישא. משבר
rashiTranslations.en: he is punishing him to death. 'tavar reisha' - breaking

rashiTranslations.he: עצמות ראש של בהמה: בקועיה.
rashiTranslations.en: the bones of an animal's head. 'bekuo'ah' -

rashiTranslations.he: בגרגרתו: סידרא. פרשת מקרא
rashiTranslations.en: in his windpipe. 'sidra' - a Scripture portion

rashiTranslations.he: של נביאים או של כתובים:
rashiTranslations.en: of the Prophets or of the Writings.

rashiTranslations.he: אתא
rashiTranslations.en: This ('he came') continues on 87b.
